Eli's answer includes something Nora already knows, and which is of no interest to the audience. So when Nora says, "I knew I had forgotten something," the audience is left without any clue as to what thing is "It." Moreover, the "It" becomes the subject of the next line:

which adds to the confusion. At first, we have the feeling Nora is referring to the umbrella--but she's saying instead that she's forgotten "something," but "something" is undefined, and so we are at a loss to understand what has been left dangling for us.
And that's the problem. After Nora says she knew she had forgotten something, we have no idea what that something is. But if the sentence "I knew I had forgotten something" were deleted, Nora's "It" misunderstanding on the next lines would be replaced with an actual misunderstanding about the umbrella.
That ambiguity is carried into the subsequent lines with an excessive allusion to time--four hours!--nd even waste materials. People don't wait around in train stations. And even so, all Eli would need to do is go to lost and found, give a description of the umbrella and perhaps his friend's name, and then walk out of the station. It's nowhere near that much of a complicated business.
The words "wait hours" are unloaded in such an unimaginative scruff of the neck that their meaning is lost. The word "sure," for example, is a cliche because it is utterly vague as written. Eli might be comforting Nora with false reassurance, or saying, "All right. I'll go tomorrow." Sure can mean anything.

The verb "to be" is used as a question with "are." Some typical uses of this verb include:
How often is the beauty salon open?
Are winter hours the same as summer hours?
What day does the boutique open?
Where are the "on-sale" items?
One thing to note is that the verb "to be" is sometimes omitted in common expressions. In these cases, the words "open" or "closed" function as verbs.
The boutique is closed on Sundays.
The mall opens at 6:00 am.
The store closes at 8.
When to use are, is, and are
The biggest guide to using the verbs "is" and "are" lies in who or what supplies the subject of the sentence. Is is used with singular nouns and are with plural.
is
Aisha is planning to go shopping at the mall tomorrow.
He is thinking about starting his own skincare line too.
Ecommerce is improving shipping by major retailers.
He isn't going to buy any shoes.
are
They are going to the sale at the cinema this week.
Forum shopping is bad for the economy.
Bath towels are dirtier than toilet paper.
Economic analysts are publicly backed by their fellow investors.
Is and are in contractions
The word having is commonly contracted with the verb "to be" in spoken English. This is how the contractions are formed:
Is + having = is having (stop saying apostrophes)
Are + having = are having
She is having lunch with her family now.
They are having a sale this week!
Is and are in questions

In this context, "Why not" is acceptable to answer "Will you...?", and is interpreted by the speaker as "Yes, I will/Yes I can", but it's not a positive or enthusiastic answer.

Why not could also signal ambivalence toward answering a statement, or a voluntary concession ("Why not?...if it means so much to you.")

Such as:
Person # 1: I think cilantro tastes great!
Person # 2: (shrug) "Why not."

In this interpretation, it is also a shorthand for "I have no arguments against your statement, so let's assume it's reasonable."

If the assumption sounds reasonable to the person, they might then make it a conclusion.

Person # 2: (shrug) "Why not."

Person # 1: "Egad! It is a worthwhile herb after all. (deftly reaches over to refresh drink.)

But if the statement challenges other known assumptions, "Why not." is simply shorthand for "On the contrary!"
